This is a little bit long winded, but I love guns and would like you to know more about the subject as well.

OP's trick would work only on an open bolt gun. Open bolt guns are designed in a way that as the bolt moves forward past the magazine, it pushes a round up out of the magazine and up into the chamber. They are almost always designed with a static firing pin on the bolt that doesn't move at all. That means that as soon as the round is in the chamber the firing pin will already be striking the primer/rim to fire that round. The expanding gases from that round immediately start pushing the bolt back to cycle the gun for the next round. This is called a "blowback" firearm.

  • With open bolt guns, if you want to fire a single shot you have to implement a mechanism to STOP the cycling process. The way you stop this process is to hold the bolt open (rearwards, or back) hence the term "open bolt"

Because of this fact, almost all open bolt guns are incredibly easy to modify in to fully automatic firearms,often you just take out that part that stops the cycling process. Because of THAT fact, almost all open bolt guns are illegal in the USA. Guns originally designed as open bolt guns, such as the Uzi or Mac 10, if the manufacturer wants to sell that firearm on the civilian market, need to be redesigned to operate from a closed bolt (not a rotating bolt as I'll explain below). Since these guns were not designed originally as closed bolt guns, these changes inevitably lead to instability and unreliability which is why you will not hear good things about civilian Uzi's or Mac 10's.

Open bolt designs are old archaic designs. They work, in the same way that a revolver still "works", but a revolver only carries 6-7 rounds and I'll take my 18 round 9mm self loading pistol over that any day the same way that I'll take my kilojoule milliwat laser pistol or whatever the fuck when it comes out in 30 years. Dinosaurs are extinct.

The AR15 is not an "open bolt" design. It is a "rotating bolt" designed with locking lugs (the little bits of metal that come off from the bolt in a star-ish like formation if we're getting really eli5 here, which if you're asking this question we are, no offense.). The lugs lock the bolt to the barrel of the gun and are completely integral to the operation of the gun (if you know anything about cars, think carburated vs fuel injected. Completely different systems.) because unlike an open bolt gun, the gas putting pressure on the bullet casing does NOT push the bolt back, which is the whole point of a locking lug system. The forces involved in the expanding gases dont affect any of the parts of the gun until the bullet is at least past the gas port of the gun (located in the front sight block of most ar15s) which will port the gases to the bolt to start the self loading cycle. This is about as accurate as you can make a self loading rifle.

  • Rotating bolt guns are designed for a single shot, if you want to fire more than one shot per trigger pull, you have to implement a mechanism to simulate a second "trigger pull" after the system has already reset itself. < this last part about the system having to be reset is important to this thread

All rotating bolt guns should have a safety in place on the firing pin so that its not even possible for the firing pin to move and fire a round unless the bolt is locked where it needs to be ("in battery" ("in battery" is a whole nother short story, just accept that its called that)). Also, locking lug guns are designed specifically to operate entirely on the gas coming through the gas port I mentioned above.

The mechanism used to simulate another trigger pull on a rotating bolt system is indeed going to use springs to push something in to place (auto seer), but that part needs to be delayed somehow to give the bolt time to push a round into the chamber and lock itself into place with the locking lugs. The best way to do this is to have the bolt carrier act as your trigger. If the bolt carrier is at a certain point on its way forward, you can release the hammer and it will reliably contact the firing pin at the moment when the bolt is locked to the barrel.

Go look up an ar15 auto seer, you'll see a flat surface that contacts the bolt carrier and a little dog leg that comes down that will kick the seer out of place as soon as the bolt carrier makes contact with it which causes the hammer to start moving forward resulting in setting off the round.

If you try to imagine the system working in OP's image, the hammer will NOT be held back while the bolt travels forward, thus, the hammer will be contacting the firing pin at some point during this travel and may or may not have enough force while following the bolt carrier forward to either a: make it past the bolt safety, or b: activate the primer.

OP's system may give you 2 rounds, hell, may give you 3, but if you boil it down its rock em sock em robots playing paddle ball and its just not worth trusting your life to this mickey mouse shit.
